title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 44
paragraphs: After this, the Lydians came bearing the corpse, and the slayer followed behind it. Taking his stand before the corpse, he gave himself up to Croesus, holding out his hands and bidding the king slay him over the corpse, speaking of his former misfortune and saying that in addition to it he had now become the destroyer of the man who had purified him of it, and that for him life was no longer worth living. But Croesus, hearing this, pitied Adrastus, although he was himself suffering so great a calamity of his own, and said to him: “Guest, I have already received from you all the satisfaction that is due, seeing that you condemn yourself to death. Nor are you alone the cause of this evil—except insofar as you were its unwilling instrument—but someone among the gods, as I suppose, who long ago signified to me what was about to happen.” So Croesus buried his son in fitting fashion. But Adrastus, son of Gordias, son of Midas—he who had been the slayer of his own brother and the slayer also of the man who had purified him—when a hush fell upon all the people around the tomb, recognizing that he was more grievously burdened by misfortune than any man he knew of, killed himself upon the grave.
